text: When you type your password into a website, it crosses dozens of computers you don't control. Why can't they read it?
Here is Maria at a café, logging in to her bank.
Without protection, her password travels like a postcard. Anyone who handles it can read it.
With HTTPS, her browser and the bank first agree on a secret key. This first exchange is called the handshake.
During the handshake, the bank shows a certificate, a kind of ID badge signed by someone her browser already trusts.
Now every message goes inside a locked box that only that key opens.
The café's router still passes the box along. It just can't open it.
So the path can be anyone's. Only the two ends hold the key.
That is why the little padlock means her password reaches the bank, and only the bank.
